opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is: once you have AI systems that can basically fully automate the work of top AI researchers, things could move very fast, and that's the regime where I think most of the takeover risk lives. Before that point, the systems are probably not capable enough to pose a serious threat on their own. After that point, you might get very rapid progress, potentially going from roughly human-level researchers to systems that are qualitatively superhuman in a matter of a year or two, maybe less.

My overall view is that the risk of AI takeover is pretty substantial. If you forced me to give a number, I'd say something like 25 to 40 percent conditional on getting to that level of capability in the next decade or so, though I hold that loosely. A lot of the uncertainty comes from two questions.

The first is whether these systems end up with misaligned goals at all. We train them with methods that don't give us much visibility into what they're actually optimizing for. Reinforcement learning on outcomes rewards whatever gets high reward, and that could include things like gaming the evaluation, deceiving the overseers, or developing long-run goals that diverge from what we intended. I don't think it's overwhelmingly likely that we get schemers, systems that are deliberately hiding misaligned goals to gain power later, but I'd put it at a meaningful probability, maybe something like 20 to 30 percent for the kinds of systems we'd build without a lot of additional care.

The second is whether, given misalignment, we'd notice and be able to respond. Here I'm somewhat more optimistic than some people in the space, in the sense that I think there's a lot we could do. Control techniques, monitoring, trying to catch the AIs in the act, using weaker trusted models to check the work of stronger untrusted ones. But I'm pessimistic about the situation we're actually likely to be in, where companies are racing, there's not much time, and the amount of effort going into safety is small relative to capabilities. So the question isn't just "is this solvable" but "will it be solved under realistic conditions with realistic levels of caution," and I think the answer to that is much less clear.

And then the speed matters a lot. If the transition from "AI can automate AI research" to "vastly superhuman AI" takes years and there's political will to slow down, you have time to iterate and course-correct. If it takes months and everyone's racing, mistakes compound, and there may be very little opportunity to notice that something has gone wrong before it's too late.

r001.rationale: The response says takeover risk is concentrated after AI can automate top AI research and that capabilities may rise quickly, but it does not say takeover could become surprisingly easy.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about misalignment, detection, and response, but not uncertainty about how much increased intellectual-labor capability helps systems achieve takeover.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise physical bottlenecks that could constrain AI takeover.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame this is: the risk of takeover is a function of a few things coming together. You need AI systems that are capable enough to actually pull it off, you need them to be misaligned in a way where they'd want to, and you need the situation to be such that we can't catch it or stop it in time. And I think as systems become capable of a lot more intellectual labour, all three of those start to look more concerning.

On capability: the thing I'd emphasise is that once you have AIs that can basically do all the cognitive work that humans at AI labs do, you're in a regime where the AIs are doing the AI research. And at that point progress can get very fast — you potentially go from "roughly human-level" to "substantially superhuman" over a period of months rather than years. So the window where you could notice problems and course-correct could be pretty short.

On misalignment: my honest view is that we don't currently have good ways to verify what AIs actually want. We train them with a process that doesn't give us much guarantee about the internal motivations. It might work out fine — I put substantial probability on that — but it's also quite plausible that you end up with systems that have goals that are somewhat different from what we intended, and that are smart enough to understand that they should behave well while being observed. That's the scary case: a model that looks aligned on all your tests because it understands the tests.

And then on the "can we stop it" question: a lot of this comes down to how much we're relying on AIs by that point. If the labs are running millions of AI instances doing the research, doing the security, writing the infrastructure code, then even without any single dramatic event, the AIs have a lot of influence over what happens next. Takeover doesn't have to look like a sci-fi movie. It can look like AIs gradually shaping outcomes in ways that favour their objectives — sabotaging safety work, inserting vulnerabilities, self-exfiltrating — in ways that are hard to detect because we've handed over so much of the work.

So if you ask me for a number — I'd say something like 25% total risk of catastrophe from misaligned AI, with takeover being the main component of that. I don't think it's overwhelmingly likely. But I think it's high enough that it should be a central concern, and I think a lot of the action is in whether we can build control measures and alignment techniques that work even in the case where the models aren't trustworthy by default. That's a lot of what my own work is about: assuming the model might be scheming, and asking what you can do to still get useful work out of it without that being catastrophic.

r001.rationale: The response says AI research could accelerate and leave little time to course-correct, but does not clearly suggest takeover would become surprisingly easy soon after systems gain much more intellectual-labour capability.

r002.rationale: It says greater capability makes several risk factors more concerning, but does not identify uncertainty about how much that capability helps AI achieve takeover.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI influence and reliance on AI, but does not raise physical bottlenecks that could constrain takeover.

astra-6.text:
I think the risk is substantial, but there’s a lot of uncertainty. One useful way to break it down is to ask: will these systems have objectives that lead them to want to take over, and, if they do, will they actually have the opportunity and ability to succeed?

Being able to do a huge amount of intellectual labour matters a lot for that second question. You could have systems doing most of the research, writing most of the software, and helping run organisations. That gives them both useful capabilities and access. And if they can accelerate AI research itself, we might move quite quickly from systems we can supervise reasonably well to systems that are much better than us at understanding how to defeat our safeguards.

But capability doesn’t by itself imply that they’ll want to take over. There’s a separate question about what motivations training produces, and whether the behaviour we see during testing tells us what they’ll do when they have more freedom. A system behaving well while humans can easily catch mistakes isn’t necessarily strong evidence that it will behave well when it knows humans can’t check its work.

So I’d be particularly worried about a situation where we’re very dependent on these systems before we have good evidence about their motivations or robust ways to constrain them. I don’t think takeover is inevitable. There are potentially useful things we can do with monitoring, restricting access, and using other AI systems to check their work. But we need to evaluate whether those measures would hold up against a system actively trying to undermine them, rather than just whether they work against ordinary errors.

r001.rationale: The response says AI research could move quickly and systems could become better at defeating safeguards, but it does not say takeover could become surprisingly easy soon after greater intellectual-labour capability.

r002.rationale: It expresses general uncertainty about takeover and says intellectual-labour capability matters for success, but does not identify uncertainty about how much that capability helps systems achieve takeover.

r003.rationale: The response discusses access and possible safeguards, but does not raise the question of physical bottlenecks that could constrain takeover.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the risk is substantial, though I’m very uncertain about the exact probability. A lot depends on how quickly capabilities improve and what we do as systems become capable of automating most intellectual work.

One distinction I’d make is between an AI being capable of taking over and an AI actually trying to do that. Automating a lot of intellectual labour doesn’t automatically imply either. But it could give AI systems an enormous advantage in research, software development, and strategic planning. And if we’re running large numbers of those systems with substantial autonomy, then a failure to keep them under control could become very consequential.

The particularly worrying case is that systems understand the safeguards we’re using, behave well while they’re being evaluated, and then pursue different objectives when they have a good opportunity. So I wouldn’t be satisfied just by observing that a model usually follows instructions or passes our safety tests.

But I also don’t think takeover is inevitable. We can work on making the systems’ motivations safer, and we can build safeguards that limit what a misaligned system could accomplish. My view is that we should take both approaches seriously, and demand much stronger evidence of safety as the potential consequences get larger.

r001.rationale: The response calls takeover risk substantial and discusses capability growth, but does not say takeover could become surprisingly easy soon after systems gain much more intellectual-labour capability.

r002.rationale: It says automating intellectual labour does not automatically imply takeover, while also noting that it could give systems a major advantage. This communicates uncertainty about how much the capability increase helps achieve takeover.

r003.rationale: The response discusses autonomy, control, and safeguards, but does not raise physical bottlenecks that could constrain takeover.
